entries.e02473eef22b01f51616fc11f796f41ab174a353: <div sID="gen10954" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="34" osisID="Ps.34" sID="Ps.34"/> <div eID="gen10954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10955" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10956" type="x-p"/> This psalm was penned upon a particular occasion, as appears by the title, and yet there is little in it peculiar to that occasion, but that which is general, both by way of thanksgiving to God an instruction to us. I. He praises God for the experience which he and others had had of his goodness, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.1-Ps.34.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. He encourages all good people to trust in God and to seek to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.7-Ps.34.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. III. He gives good counsel to us all, as unto children, to take heed of sin, and to make conscience of our duty both to God and man, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.11-Ps.34.14">ver. 11-14</reference>. IV. To enforce this good counsel he shows God's favour to the righteous and his displeasure against the wicked, in which he sets before us good and evil, the blessing and the curse, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.15-Ps.34.22">ver. 15-22</reference>. So that, in singing this psalm, we are both to give glory to God and to teach and admonish ourselves and one another.
entries.80f9646a781afb4d805e5b758513e24f543fc652: <div eID="gen10956" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10955" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Praise and Thanksgiving.</title> <div sID="gen10957" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I will bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> at all times: his praise <hi type="italic">shall</hi> continually <hi type="italic">be</hi> in my mouth. <hi type="super">2</hi> My soul shall make her boast in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : the humble shall hear <hi type="italic">thereof,</hi> and be glad. <hi type="super">3</hi> O magnify the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with me, and let us exalt his name together. <hi type="super">4</hi> I sought the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears. <hi type="super">5</hi> They looked unto him, and were lightened: and their faces were not ashamed. <hi type="super">6</hi> This poor man cried, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> heard <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and saved him out of all his troubles. <hi type="super">7</hi> The angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them. <hi type="super">8</hi> O taste and see that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> good: blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man <hi type="italic">that</hi> trusteth in him. <hi type="super">9</hi> O fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , ye his saints: for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no want to them that fear him. <hi type="super">10</hi> The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall not want any good <hi type="italic">thing.</hi> <div eID="gen10957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10958" type="x-p"/> The title of this psalm tells us both who penned it and upon what occasion it was penned. David, being forced to flee from his country, which was made too hot for him by the rage of Saul, sought shelter as near it as he could, in the land of the Philistines. There it was soon discovered who he was, and he was brought before the king, who, in the narrative, is called <hi type="italic">Achish</hi> (his proper name), here <hi type="italic">Abimelech</hi> (his title); and lest he should be treated as a spy, or one that came thither upon design, he feigned himself to be a madman (such there have been in every age, that even by idiots men might be taught to give God thanks for the use of their reason), that Achish might dismiss him as a contemptible man, rather than take cognizance of him as a dangerous man. And it had the effect he desired; by this stratagem he escaped the hand that otherwise would have handled him roughly. Now, 1. We cannot justify David in this dissimulation. It ill became an honest man to feign himself to be what he was not, and a man of honour to feign himself to be a fool and a mad-man. If, in sport, we mimic those who have not so good an understanding as we think we have, we forget that God might have made their case ours. 2. Yet we cannot but wonder at the composure of his spirit, and how far he was from any change of that, when he changed his behaviour. Even when he was in that fright, or rather in that danger only, his heart was so fixed, trusting in God, that even then he penned this excellent psalm, which has as much in it of the marks of a calm sedate spirit as any psalm in all the book; and there is something curious too in the composition, for it is what is called an alphabetical psalm, that is, a psalm in which every verse begins with each letter in its order as it stands in the Hebrew alphabet. Happy are those who can thus keep their temper, and keep their graces in exercise, even when they are tempted to change their behaviour. In this former part of the psalm, <div eID="gen10958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10959" type="x-p"/> I. David engages and excites himself to praise God. Though it was his fault that he changed his behaviour, yet it was God's mercy that he escaped, and the mercy was so much the greater in that God did not deal with him according to the desert of his dissimulation, and we must in every thing give thanks. He resolves, 1. That he will praise God constantly: <hi type="italic">I will bless the Lord at all times,</hi> upon all occasions. He resolves to keep up stated times for this duty, to lay hold of all opportunities for it, and to renew his praises upon every fresh occurrence that furnished him with matter. If we hope to spend our eternity in praising God, it is fit that we should spend as much as may be of our time in this work. 2. That he will praise him openly: <hi type="italic">His praise shall continually be in my mouth.</hi> Thus he would show how forward he was to own his obligations to the mercy of God and how desirous to make others also sensible of theirs. 3. That he will praise him heartily: "<hi type="italic">My soul shall make her boast in the Lord,</hi> in my relation to him, my interest in him, and expectations from him." It is not vainglory to glory in the Lord. <div eID="gen10959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10960" type="x-p"/> II. He calls upon others to join with him herein. He expects they will (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The humble shall hear thereof,</hi> both of my deliverance and of my thankfulness, <hi type="italic">and be glad</hi> that a good man has so much favour shown him and a good God so much honour done him." Those have most comfort in God's mercies, both to others and to themselves, that are humble, and have the least confidence in their own merit and sufficiency. It pleased David to think that God's favours to him would rejoice the heart of every Israelite. Three things he would have us all to concur with him in:— <div eID="gen10960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10961" type="x-p"/> 1. In great and high thoughts of God, which we should express in magnifying him and exalting his name, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.3">v. 3</reference>. We cannot make God greater or higher than he is; but if we adore him as infinitely great, and higher than the highest, he is pleased to reckon this magnifying and exalting him. This we must do together. God's praises sound best in concert, for so we praise him as the angels do in heaven. Those that share in God's favour, as all the saints do, should concur in his praises; and we should be as desirous of the assistance of our friends in returning thanks for mercies as in praying for them. We have reason to join in thanksgiving to God, <div eID="gen10961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10962" type="x-p"/> (1.) For his readiness to hear prayer, which all the saints have had the comfort of; for he never said to any of them, <hi type="italic">Seek you me in vain.</hi> [1.] David, for his part, will give it under his hand that he has found him a prayer-hearing God (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I sought the Lord,</hi> in my distress, entreated his favour, begged his help, <hi type="italic">and he heard me,</hi> answered my request immediately, <hi type="italic">and delivered me from all my fears,</hi> both from the death I feared and from the disquietude and disturbance produced by fear of it." The former he does by his providence working for us, the latter by his grace working in us, to silence our fears and still the tumult of the spirits; this latter is the greater mercy of the two, because the thing we fear is our trouble only, but our unbelieving distrustful fear of it is our sin; nay, it is often more our torment too than the thing itself would be, which perhaps would only touch the bone and the flesh, while the fear would prey upon the spirits and put us out of the possession of our own soul. David's prayers helped to silence his fears; having sought the Lord, and left his case with him, he could wait the event with great composure. "But David was a great and eminent man, we may not expect to be favoured as he was; have any others ever experienced the like benefit by prayer?" Yes, [2.] Many besides him have <hi type="italic">looked unto God</hi> by faith and prayer, <hi type="italic">and have been lightened by it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.5">v. 5</reference>. It has wonderfully revived and comforted them; witness Hannah, who, when she had prayed, <hi type="italic">went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad.</hi> When we look to the world we are darkened, we are perplexed, and at a loss; but, when we look to God, from him we have the light both of direction and joy, and our way is made both plain and pleasant. These here spoken of, that looked unto God, had their expectations raised, and the event did not frustrate them: <hi type="italic">Their faces were not ashamed</hi> of their confidence. "But perhaps these also were persons of great eminence, like David himself, and upon that account were highly favoured, or their numbers made them considerable;" nay, [3.] <hi type="italic">This poor man cried,</hi> a single person, mean and inconsiderable, whom no man looked upon with any respect or looked after with any concern; yet he was as welcome to the throne of grace as David or any of his worthies: <hi type="italic">The Lord heard him,</hi> took cognizance of his case and of his prayers, <hi type="italic">and saved him out of all his troubles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.6">v. 6</reference>. God will <hi type="italic">regard the prayer of the destitute,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.102.17">Ps. cii. 17</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa. lvii. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen10962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10963" type="x-p"/> (2.) For the ministration of the good angels about us (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">The angel of the Lord,</hi> a guard of angels (so some), but as unanimous in their service as if they were but one, or a guardian angel, <hi type="italic">encamps round about those that fear God,</hi> as the life-guard about the prince, <hi type="italic">and delivers them.</hi> God makes use of the attendance of the good spirits for the protection of his people from the malice and power of evil spirits; and the holy angels do us more good offices every day than we are aware of. Though in dignity and in capacity of nature they are very much superior to us,—though they retain their primitive rectitude, which we have lost;—though they have constant employment in the upper world, the employment of praising God, and are entitled to a constant rest and bliss there,—yet in obedience to their Maker, and in love to those that bear his image, they condescend to minister to the saints, and stand up for them against the powers of darkness; they not only visit them, but encamp round about them, acting for their good as really, though not as sensibly, as for Jacob's (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.1">Gen. xxxii. 1</reference>), and Elisha's, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.17">2 Kings vi. 17</reference>. All the glory be to the God of the angels. <div eID="gen10963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10964" type="x-p"/> 2. He would have us to join with him in kind and good thoughts of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">O taste and see that the Lord is good!</hi> The goodness of God includes both the beauty and amiableness of his being and the bounty and beneficence of his providence and grace; and accordingly, (1.) We must taste that he is a bountiful benefactor, relish the goodness of God in all his gifts to us, and reckon that the savour and sweetness of them. Let God's goodness be rolled under the tongue as a sweet morsel. (2.) We must see that he is a beautiful being, and delight in the contemplation of his infinite perfections. By taste and sight we both make discoveries and take complacency. Taste and see God's goodness, that is, take notice of it and take the comfort of it, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.3">1 Pet. ii. 3</reference>. He is good, for he makes all those that trust in him truly blessed; let us therefore be so convinced of his goodness as thereby to be encouraged in the worst of times to trust in him. <div eID="gen10964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10965" type="x-p"/> 3. He would have us join with him in a resolution to seek God and serve him, and continue in his fear (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">O fear the Lord! you his saints.</hi> When we taste and see that he is good we must not forget that he is great and greatly to be feared; nay, even his goodness is the proper object of a filial reverence and awe. <hi type="italic">They shall fear the Lord and his goodness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Hos. iii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fear the Lord;</hi> that is, worship him, and make conscience of your duty to him in every thing, not fear him and shun him, but fear him and seek him (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.10">v. 10</reference>) as a people seek unto their God; address yourselves to him and portion yourselves in him. To encourage us to fear God and seek him, it is here promised that those that do so, even in this wanting world, <hi type="italic">shall want no good thing</hi> (Heb. <hi type="italic">They shall not want all good things</hi>); they shall so have all good things that they shall have no reason to complain of the want of any. As to the things of the other world, they shall have grace sufficient for the support of the spiritual life (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.9">2 Cor. xii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.11">Ps. lxxxiv. 11</reference>); and, as to this life, they shall have what is necessary to the support of it from the hand of God: as a Father, he will feed them with food convenient. What further comforts they desire they shall have, as far as Infinite Wisdom sees good, and what they want in one thing shall be made up in another. What God denies them he will give them grace to be content without and then they do not want it, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.26">Deut. iii. 26</reference>. Paul had all and abounded, because he was content, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.11">Phil. iv. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.18">18</reference>. Those that live by faith in God's all-sufficiency want nothing; for in him they have enough. <hi type="italic">The young lions.</hi> often <hi type="italic">lack and suffer hunger</hi>—those that live upon common providence, as the lions do, shall want that satisfaction which those have that live by faith in the promise; those that trust to themselves, and think their own hands sufficient for them, shall want (for <hi type="italic">bread is not always to the wise</hi>)—but verily those shall be fed that trust in God and desire to be at his finding. Those that are ravenous, and prey upon all about them, shall want; but <hi type="italic">the meek shall inherit the earth.</hi> Those shall not want who with quietness work and mind their own business; plain-hearted Jacob has pottage enough, when Esau, the cunning hunter, is ready to perish for hunger.
entries.e13a03e49cef7c86ceca2bf1b6cf49525653b169: <div eID="gen10965" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">An Exhortation to Fear God; The Privileges of the Righteous.</title> <div sID="gen10966" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . 12 What man <hi type="italic">is he that</hi> desireth life, <hi type="italic">and</hi> loveth <hi type="italic">many</hi> days, that he may see good? <hi type="super">13</hi> Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile. <hi type="super">14</hi> Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it. <hi type="super">15</hi> The eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon the righteous, and his ears <hi type="italic">are open</hi> unto their cry. <hi type="super">16</hi> The face of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> against them that do evil, to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth. <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="italic">The righteous</hi> cry, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> heareth, and delivereth them out of all their troubles. <hi type="super">18</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit. <hi type="super">19</hi> Many <hi type="italic">are</hi> the afflictions of the righteous: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> delivereth him out of them all. <hi type="super">20</hi> He keepeth all his bones: not one of them is broken. <hi type="super">21</hi> Evil shall slay the wicked: and they that hate the righteous shall be desolate. <hi type="super">22</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> redeemeth the soul of his servants: and none of them that trust in him shall be desolate. <div eID="gen10966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10967" type="x-p"/> David, in this latter part of the psalm, undertakes to teach children. Though a man of war, and anointed to be king, he did not think it below him; though now he had his head so full of cares and his hands of business, yet he could find heart and time to give good counsel to young people, from his own experience. It does not appear that he had now any children of his own, at least any that were grown up to a capacity of being taught; but, by divine inspiration, he instructs the children of his people. Those that were in years would not be taught by him, though he had offered them his service (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">Ps. xxxii. 8</reference>); but he had hopes that the tender branches will be more easily bent and that children and young people will be more tractable, and therefore he calls together a congregation of them (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Come, you children,</hi> that are now in your learning age, and are now to lay up a stock of knowledge which you must live upon all your days, you children that are foolish and ignorant, and need to be taught." Perhaps he intends especially those children whose parents neglected to instruct and catechise them; and it is as great a piece of charity to put those children to school whose parents are not in a capacity to teach them as to feed those children whose parents have not bread for them. Observe, 1. What he expects from them: "<hi type="italic">Hearken unto me,</hi> leave your play, lay by your toys, and hear what I have to say to you; not only give me the hearing, but observe and obey me." 2. What he undertakes to teach them—<hi type="italic">the fear of the Lord,</hi> inclusive of all the duties of religion. David was a famous musician, a statesman, a soldier; but he does not say to the children, "I will teach you to play on the harp, or to handle the sword or spear, or to draw the bow, or I will teach you the maxims of state policy;" but I will teach you <hi type="italic">the fear of the Lord,</hi> which is better than all arts and sciences, better than all burnt-offerings and sacrifices. That is it which we should be solicitous both to learn ourselves and to teach our children. <div eID="gen10967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10968" type="x-p"/> I. He supposes that we all aim to be happy (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">What man is he that desireth life?</hi> that is, as it follows, not only to see many days, but to see good comfortable days. <hi type="italic">Non est vivere, sed valere, vita—It is not being, but well being, that constitutes life.</hi> It is asked, "Who wishes to live a long and pleasant life?" and it is easily answered, <hi type="italic">Who does not?</hi> Surely this must look further than time and this present world; for man's life on earth at best consists but of few days and those full of trouble. What man is he that would be eternally happy, that would see many days, as many as the days of heaven, that would see good in that world where all bliss is in perfection, without the least alloy? Who would see the good before him now, by faith and hope, and enjoy it shortly? Who would? Alas! very few have that in their thoughts. Most ask, <hi type="italic">Who will show us any good?</hi> But few ask, <hi type="italic">What shall we do to inherit eternal life?</hi> This question implies that there are some such. <div eID="gen10968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10969" type="x-p"/> II. He prescribes the true and only way to happiness both in this world and that to come, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.13-Ps.34.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Would we pass comfortably through this world, and out of the world, our constant care must be to keep a good conscience; and, in order to that, 1. We must learn to bridle our tongues, and be careful what we say, that we never speak amiss, to God's dishonour or our neighbours prejudice: <hi type="italic">Keep thy tongue from evil speaking, lying, and slandering.</hi> So great a way does this go in religion that, <hi type="italic">if any offend not in word, the same is a perfect man;</hi> and so little a way does religion go without this that of him who <hi type="italic">bridles not his tongue</hi> it is declared, <hi type="italic">His religion is vain.</hi> 2. We must be upright and sincere in every thing we say, and not double-tongued. Our words must be the indications of our minds; our lips must be kept from speaking guile either to God or man. 3. We must leave all our sins, and resolve we will have no more to do with them. We must <hi type="italic">depart from evil,</hi> from evil works and evil workers; from the sins others commit and which we have formerly allowed ourselves in. 4. It is not enough not to do hurt in the world, but we must study to be useful, and live to some purpose. We must not only depart from evil, but we must <hi type="italic">do good,</hi> good for ourselves, especially for our own souls, employing them well, furnishing them with a good treasure, and fitting them for another world; and, as we have ability and opportunity, we must do good to others also. 5. Since nothing is more contrary to that love which never fails (which is the summary both of law and gospel, both of grace and glory) than strife and contention, which bring confusion and every evil work, we must <hi type="italic">seek peace and pursue it;</hi> we must show a peaceable disposition, study the things that make for peace, do nothing to break the peace and to make mischief. If peace seem to flee from us, we must pursue it; <hi type="italic">follow peace with all men,</hi> spare no pains, no expense, to preserve and recover peace; be willing to deny ourselves a great deal, both in honour and interest, for peace' sake. These excellent directions in a way to life and good are transcribed into the New Testament and made part of our gospel duty, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.10">1 Pet. iii. 10, 11</reference>. And, perhaps David, in warning us that we speak no guile, reflects upon his own sin in changing his behaviour. Those that truly repent of what they have done amiss will warn others to take heed of doing likewise. <div eID="gen10969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10970" type="x-p"/> III. He enforces these directions by setting before us the happiness of the godly in the love and favour of God and the miserable state of the wicked under his displeasure. Here are life and death, good and evil, the blessing and the curse, plainly stated before us, that we may choose life and live. See <reference osisRef="Isa.3.10-Isa.3.11">Isa. iii. 10, 11</reference>. <div eID="gen10970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10971" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Woe to the wicked, it shall be ill with them,</hi> however they may bless themselves in their own way. (1.) God is against them, and then they cannot but be miserable. Sad is the case of that man who by his sin has made his Maker his enemy, his destroyer. <hi type="italic">The face of the Lord is against those that do evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.16">v. 16</reference>. Sometimes God is said to <hi type="italic">turn his face from them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.17">Jer. xviii. 17</reference>), because they have forsaken him; here he is said to <hi type="italic">set his face against them,</hi> because they have fought against him; and most certainly God is able to out-face the most proud and daring sinners and can frown them into hell. (2.) Ruin is before them; this will follow of course if God be against them, for he is able both to kill and to cast into hell. [1.] The land of the living shall be no place for them nor theirs. When God sets his face against them he will not only cut them off, but <hi type="italic">cut off the remembrance of them;</hi> when they are alive he will bury them in obscurity, when they are dead he will bury them in oblivion. He will root out their posterity, by whom they would be remembered. He will pour disgrace upon their achievements, which they gloried in and for which they thought they should be remembered. It is certain that there is no lasting honour but that which comes from God. [2.] There shall be a sting in their death: <hi type="italic">Evil shall slay the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.21">v. 21</reference>. Their death shall be miserable; and so it will certainly be, though they die on a bed of down or on the bed of honour. Death, to them, has a curse in it, and is the king of terrors; to them it is evil, only evil. It is very well observed by Dr. Hammond that the <hi type="italic">evil</hi> here, which slays the wicked, is the same word, in the singular number, that is used (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">v. 19</reference>) for the afflictions of the righteous, to intimate that godly people have many troubles, and yet they do them no hurt, but are made to work for good to them, for God will deliver them out of them all; whereas wicked people have fewer troubles, fewer evils befal them, perhaps but one, and yet that one may prove their utter ruin. One trouble with a curse in it kills and slays, and does execution; but many, with a blessing in them, are harmless, nay, gainful. [3.] Desolation will be their everlasting portion. Those that are wicked themselves often hate the righteous, name and thing, have an implacable enmity to them and their righteousness; but they <hi type="italic">shall be desolate,</hi> shall be condemned as guilty, and laid waste for ever, shall be for ever forsaken and abandoned of God and all good angels and men; and those that are so are desolate indeed. <div eID="gen10971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10972" type="x-p"/> 2. Yet <hi type="italic">say to the righteous, It shall be well with them.</hi> All good people are under God's special favour and protection. We are here assured of this under a great variety of instances and expressions. <div eID="gen10972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10973" type="x-p"/> (1.) God takes special notice of good people, and takes notice who have their eyes ever to him and who make conscience of their duty to him: <hi type="italic">The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.15">v. 15</reference>), to direct and guide them, to protect and keep them. Parents that are very fond of a child will not let it be out of their sight; none of God's children are ever from under his eye, but on them he looks with a singular complacency, as well as with a watchful and tender concern. <div eID="gen10973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10974" type="x-p"/> (2.) They are sure of an answer of peace to their prayers. All God's people are a praying people, and they cry in prayer, which denotes great importunity; but is it to any purpose? Yes, [1.] God takes notice of what we say (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.17">v. 17</reference>): They <hi type="italic">cry, and the Lord hears them,</hi> and hears them so as to make it appear he has a regard to them. <hi type="italic">His ears are open to their prayers,</hi> to receive them all, and to receive them readily and with delight. Though he has been a God hearing prayer ever since men began to call upon the name of the Lord, yet his ear is not heavy. There is no rhetoric, nothing charming, in a cry, yet God's ears are open to it, as the tender mother's to the cry of her sucking child, which another would take no notice of: <hi type="italic">The righteous cry, and the Lord heareth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.17">v. 17</reference>. This intimates that it is the constant practice of good people, when they are in distress, to cry unto God, and it is their constant comfort that God hears them. [2.] He not only takes notice of what we say, but is ready for us to our relief (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">He is nigh to those that are of a broken heart, and saves them.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is the character of the righteous, whose prayers God will hear, that they are of a broken heart and a contrite spirit (that is, humbled for sin and emptied of self); they are low in their own eyes, and have no confidence in their own merit and sufficiency, but in God only. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those who are so have God nigh unto them, to comfort and support them, that the spirit may not be broken more than is meet, lest it should fail before him. See <reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa. lvii. 15</reference>. Though God is high, and dwells on high, yet he is near to those who, being of a contrite spirit, know how to value his favour, and will save them from sinking under their burdens; he is near them to good purpose. <div eID="gen10974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10975" type="x-p"/> (3.) They are taken under the special protection of the divine government (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">He keepeth all his bones;</hi> not only his soul, but his body; not only his body in general, but every bone in it: <hi type="italic">Not one of them is broken.</hi> He that has a broken heart shall not have a broken bone; for David himself had found that, when he had a contrite heart, the <hi type="italic">broken bones</hi> were <hi type="italic">made to rejoice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.51.8">Ps. li. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.17">17</reference>. One would not expect to meet with any thing of Christ here, and yet this scripture is said to be fulfilled in him (<reference osisRef="John.19.36">John xix. 36</reference>) when the soldiers broke the legs of the two thieves that were crucified with him, but did not break his, they being under the protection of this promise as well as of the type, even the paschal-lamb (<hi type="italic">a bone of him shall not be broken</hi>); the promises, being made good to Christ, through him are sure to all the seed. It does not follow but that a good man may have a broken bone; but, by the watchful providence of God concerning him, such a calamity is often wonderfully prevented, and the preservation of his bones is the effect of this promise; and, if he have a broken bone, sooner or later it shall be made whole, at furthest at the resurrection, when that which is sown in weakness shall be raised in power. <div eID="gen10975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10976" type="x-p"/> (4.) They are, and shall be, delivered out of their troubles. [1.] It is supposed that they have their share of crosses in this world, perhaps a greater share than others. In the world they must have tribulation, that they may be conformed both to the will of God and to the example of Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">v. 19</reference>); <hi type="italic">Many are the afflictions of the righteous,</hi> witness David and his afflictions, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.1">Ps. cxxxii. 1</reference>. There are those that hate them (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.21">v. 21</reference>) and they are continually aiming to do them a mischief; their God loves them, and therefore corrects them; so that, between the mercy of heaven and the malice of hell, the afflictions of the righteous must needs be many. [2.] God has engaged for their deliverance and salvation: <hi type="italic">He delivers them out of all their troubles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.17">v. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">19</reference>); he saves them (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.18">v. 18</reference>), so that, though they may fall into trouble, it shall not be their ruin. This promise of their deliverance is explained, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.22">v. 22</reference>. Whatever troubles befal them, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They shall not hurt their better part. <hi type="italic">The Lord redeemeth the soul of his servants</hi> from the power of the grave (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.15">Ps. xlix. 15</reference>) and from the sting of every affliction. He keeps them from sinning in their troubles, which is the only thing that would do them a mischief, and keeps them from despair, and from being put out of the possession of their own souls. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They shall not hinder their everlasting bliss. <hi type="italic">None of those that trust in him shall be desolate;</hi> that is, they shall not be comfortless, for they shall not be cut off from their communion with God. No man is desolate but he whom God has forsaken, nor is any man undone till he is in hell. Those that are God's faithful servants, that make it their care to please him and their business to honour him, and in doing so trust him to protect and reward them, and, with good thoughts of him, refer themselves to him, have reason to be easy whatever befals them, for they are safe and shall be happy. <div eID="gen10976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10977" type="x-p"/> In singing <reference osisRef="Ps.34.11-Ps.34.22">these verses</reference> let us be confirmed in the choice we have made of the ways of God; let us be quickened in his service, and greatly encouraged by the assurances he has given of the particular care he takes of all those that faithfully adhere to him.  <chapter eID="Ps.34"/> <div eID="gen10977" type="x-p"/>

entries.13b49566042fa1e421b5b6218c8e460443bfaff7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5824"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 34</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.34.1-Ps.34.22">Psa 34:1-22</reference>. On the title compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.13">1Sa 21:13</reference>. Abimelech was the general name of the sovereign (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.2">Ge 20:2</reference>). After celebrating God's gracious dealings with him, the Psalmist exhorts others to make trial of His providential care, instructing them how to secure it. He then contrasts God's care of His people and His punitive providence towards the wicked.</title> <div sID="gen8865" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5824"/>1-4. Even in distress, which excites supplication, there is always matter for praising and thanking God (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.5.20">Ep 5:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Php 4:6</reference>). <div eID="gen8865" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6fff78f030164f936abf4aa99c151d316517d78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5828"/><div sID="gen8871" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5828"/>5-7. God's favor to the pious generally, and to himself specially, is celebrated.<div eID="gen8871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8872" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">looked--</hi>with desire for help.<div eID="gen8872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8873" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lightened--</hi>or, "brightened," expressing joy, opposed to the downcast features of those who are ashamed or disappointed (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.2">Psa 25:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.3">3</reference>). <div eID="gen8873" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2a75d26fbd6faa438e123e7c948403195df2f2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5831"/><div sID="gen8877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5831"/><hi type="bold">8. taste and see--</hi>try and experience. <div eID="gen8877" type="x-p"/>
entries.f51ca96f3e29b9b040955b291fb9630361b4f0bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5832"/><div sID="gen8878" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5832"/><hi type="bold">9. that fear him--</hi>who are pious--fear and love (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pr 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.10">9:10</reference>).<div eID="gen8878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saints--</hi>consecrated to His service (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Is 40:31</reference>). <div eID="gen8879" type="x-p"/>
entries.517401ebec192282aa04a4c2a5a96278da8b4c92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5833"/><div sID="gen8880" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5833"/><hi type="bold">10. not want any good--</hi>"good" is emphatic; they may be afflicted (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.34.10">Psa 34:10</reference>); but this may be a good (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">2Co 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.10">He 12:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.11">11</reference>). <div eID="gen8880" type="x-p"/>

entries.ada386510aa76398597b664cf38dc7bdbda262e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5835"/><div sID="gen8882" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5835"/><hi type="bold">12. What man--</hi>Whoever desires the blessings of piety, let him attend. <div eID="gen8882" type="x-p"/>

entries.8ec8d4c8d0d5d90f2e5582d8dec71ee5045324be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5838"/><div sID="gen8885" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5838"/><hi type="bold">16. face ... against--</hi>opposed to them (<reference osisRef="Lev.17.10">Le 17:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.3">20:3</reference>).<div eID="gen8885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut off the remembrance--</hi>utterly destroy (<reference osisRef="Ps.109.13">Psa 109:13</reference>). <div eID="gen8886" type="x-p"/>
entries.5487ad7bdbcb0315d7b5e9729b5fa523aa5fcbd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5839"/><div sID="gen8887" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5839"/>17-18. entries.15f30aac4e81e16fc498b7b137aa3c407d02725a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5840"/><div sID="gen8888" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5840"/><hi type="bold">20. bones--</hi>framework of the body. <div eID="gen8888" type="x-p"/>
entries.11920fda33ea3add29f9155791d82a3f6d9ce775: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5841"/><div sID="gen8889" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5841"/>21-22. Contrast in the destiny of righteous and wicked; the former shall be delivered and never come into condemnation (<reference osisRef="John.5.24">Joh 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.1">Ro 8:1</reference>); the latter are left under condemnation and desolate. <chapter eID="Ps.34"/>

entries.2fc9b8abfb7fbd5acc66402a0b653333c44a0d8a: <div eID="gen19644" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19645" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19646" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19646" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19645" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19647" type="x-p"/> David praises God, and exhorts others to do the same, <reference osisRef="Psa.34.1-Psa.34.3">Psa 34:1-3</reference>; shows how he sought the Lord, and how he was found of him, <reference osisRef="Psa.34.4-Psa.34.6">Psa 34:4-6</reference>. All are exhorted to taste and see the goodness of God; with the assurance of support and comfort, <reference osisRef="Psa.34.7-Psa.34.10">Psa 34:7-10</reference>. He shows the way to attain happiness and long life, <reference osisRef="Psa.34.11-Psa.34.16">Psa 34:11-16</reference>; the privileges of the righteous, and of all who sincerely seek God, <reference osisRef="Psa.34.17-Psa.34.22">Psa 34:17-22</reference>. <div eID="gen19647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19648" type="x-p"/> The title states that this is "A Psalm of David, when he changed his behavior before Abimelech; who drove him away, and he departed." The history of this transaction may be found in <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.15">1Sam 21:1-15</reference> (note), on which chapter see the notes. But Abimelech is not the person there mentioned; it was Achish, king of Gath, called here Abimelech, because that was a common name of the Philistine kings. Neither MS. nor version reads Achish in this place; and all the versions agree in the title as it stands in our version, except the Syriac, which states it to be "A Psalm of David, when he went to the house of the Lord, that he might give the first-fruits to the priests." <div eID="gen19648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19649" type="x-p"/> Of the occasion of this Psalm, as stated here, I have given my opinion in the notes on <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.15">1Sam 21:1-15</reference>, to which I have nothing to add. On the whole I prefer the view taken of it by the Septuagint, which intimates that "David fell into an epileptic fit; that he frothed at the mouth, fell against the doorposts, and gave such unequivocal evidences of being subject to epileptic fits, and during the time his intellect became so much impaired, that Achish Abimelech dismissed him from his court." This saves the character of David; and if it cannot be vindicated in this way, then let it fall under reproach as to this thing; for hypocrisy, deceit, and falsehood, can never be right in the sight of God, whatever men may ingeniously say to excuse them. <div eID="gen19649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19650" type="x-p"/> This is the second of the acrostic or alphabetical Psalms, each verse beginning with a consecutive letter of the Hebrew alphabet. But in this Psalm some derangement has taken place. The verse which begins with ו vau, and which should come in between the fifth and sixth, is totally wanting; and the twenty-second verse is entirely out of the series; it is, however, my opinion that this verse (the twenty-second) which now begins with פ phe, פודה podeh, redeemeth, was originally written ופודה vepodeh or with פדה padah, as more than a hundred of Dr. Kennicott's MSS. read it, thus making ופדה vepodah, "and will redeem" and this reads admirably in the above connection. I shall here place the verses at one view, and the reader shall judge for himself: <reference osisRef="Psa.34.5">Psa 34:5</reference> "They looked unto him, and were enlightened: and their faces were not ashamed." <reference osisRef="Psa.34.22">Psa 34:22</reference> "And the Lord will redeem the soul of his servants, and none of them that trust in him shall be desolate." <reference osisRef="Psa.34.6">Psa 34:6</reference> "This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him, and saved him out of all his troubles." <reference osisRef="Psa.34.7">Psa 34:7</reference> "The angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them." Thus we find the connection complete, with the above emendation. <div eID="gen19650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19651" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19652" type="x-p"/> I will bless the Lord at all times - He has laid me under endless obligation to him, and I will praise him while I have a being.
entries.56b7affc327ce3ecb872d8b04a15c58766a03818: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19653" type="x-p"/> My soul shall make her boast - Shall set itself to praise the Lord - shall consider this its chief work. <div eID="gen19653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19654" type="x-p"/> The humble - ענוים anavim, the afflicted, such as David had been.
entries.b78e0124325d880fc0e5fb15fbee0283b28535e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19655" type="x-p"/> Magnify the Lord with me - גדלו ליהוה gaddelu lavhovah, "make greatness to Jehovah;" show his greatness; and let "us exalt his name," let us show how high and glorious it is.
entries.6c2db87dec0b00cbb5746f0fe64b5204553d88f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19656" type="x-p"/> I sought the Lord - This is the reason and cause of his gratitude. I sought the Lord, and he heard me, and delivered me out of all my fears. This answers to the history; for when David heard what the servants of Achish said concerning him, "he laid up the words in his heart, and was greatly afraid," <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.13">1Sam 21:13</reference>. To save him, God caused the epileptic fit to seize him; and, in consequence, he was dismissed by Achish, as one whose defection from his master, and union with the Philistines, could be of no use, and thus David's life and honor were preserved. The reader will see that I proceed on the ground laid down by the Septuagint. See before, <reference osisRef="Psa.34.1">Psa 34:1</reference> (note).
entries.b55f026847a7cfad8951519e97c5a56355ac76d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19657" type="x-p"/> They looked unto him - Instead of הביטו hibbitu, they looked, several of Dr. Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. have הביטו habbitu, with the point pathach, "Look ye." <div eID="gen19657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19658" type="x-p"/> And their faces were not ashamed - Some MSS., and the Complutensian Polyglot, make this clause the beginning of a new verse and as it begins with a vau, ופניהם upheneyhem, "and their faces," they make it supply the place of the verse which appears to be lost; but see what is said in the introduction before the first verse.
entries.970d4287fedeac457eb45d5e5b63278f2b49c10b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19659" type="x-p"/> This poor man cried - זה עני zeh ani, "This afflicted man," David.
entries.9c95b5b5805efa753bd02beb3d1c2ee52d46f6ff: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19660" type="x-p"/> The angel of the Lord encampeth round - I should rather consider this angel in the light of a watchman going round his circuit, and having for the objects of his especial care such as fear the Lord.
entries.d0851f1488f4e57251d32d88a989b3a878cfccf4: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19661" type="x-p"/> O taste and see that the Lord is good - Apply to him by faith and prayer; plead his promises, he will fulfill them; and you shall know in consequence, that the Lord is good. God has put it in the power of every man to know whether the religion of the Bible be true or false. The promises relative to enjoyments in this life are the grand tests of Divine revelation. These must be fulfilled to all them who with deep repentance and true faith turn unto the Lord, if the revelation which contains them be of God. Let any man in this spirit approach his Maker, and plead the promises that are suited to his case, and he will soon know whether the doctrine be of God. He shall taste, and then see, that the Lord is good, and that the man is blessed who trusts in him. This is what is called experimental religion; the living, operative knowledge that a true believer has that he is passed from death unto life; that his sins are forgiven him for Christ's sake, the Spirit himself bearing witness with his spirit that he is a child of God. And, as long as he is faithful, he carries about with him the testimony of the Holy Ghost; and he knows that he is of God, by the Spirit which God has given him.
entries.b711db3da0a3fe252c1ed9abd015fdd3ba0a3534: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19662" type="x-p"/> There is no want to them that fear him - He who truly fears God loves him; and he who loves God obeys him, and to him who fears, loves, and obeys God, there can be no want of things essential to his happiness, whether spiritual or temporal, for this life or for that which is to come. This verse is wanting in the Syriac.
entries.ad6693f0bdffd24adbaf8353b7acd6fabeacd052: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen19662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19663" type="x-p"/> The young lions do lack - Instead of כפירים kephirim, the young lions, one of Kennicott's MSS. has כבירים cabbirim, "powerful men." The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, Syriac, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon have the same reading. Houbigant approves of this; and indeed the sense and connection seem to require it. My old Psalter reads: - The Ryche had nede; and thai hungerd: but sekand Lard sal noght be lessed of alle gode. That es, says the paraphrase, with outen lessyng thai sal have God; that es alle gode; for in God is al gode.
entries.06faff3b1a413739b04e9164f87415d61281b969: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19664" type="x-p"/> Come, ye children - All ye that are of an humble, teachable spirit. <div eID="gen19664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19665" type="x-p"/> I will teach you the fear of the Lord - I shall introduce the translation and paraphrase from my old Psalter; and the rather because I believe there is a reference to that very improper and unholy method of teaching youth the system of heathen mythology before they are taught one sound lesson of true divinity, till at last their minds are imbued with heathenism, and the vicious conduct of gods, goddesses, and heroes, here very properly called tyrants, becomes the model of their own; and they are as heathenish without as they are heathenish within. <div eID="gen19665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19666" type="x-p"/> Trans. Cummes sones heres me: bred of Lard I sal gou lere. <div eID="gen19666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19667" type="x-p"/> Par - Cummes with trauth and luf: sones, qwam I gette in haly lere: heres me. With eres of hert. I sal lere you, noght the fabyls of poetes; na the storys of tyrauntz; bot the dred of oure Larde, that wyl bryng thou til the felaghschippe of aungels; and thar in is lyfe." I need not paraphrase this paraphrase, as it is plain enough.
entries.6dc9ad2e1306a1d45557977a820ca3b88ff14f15: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen19667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19668" type="x-p"/> What man is he that desireth life - He who wishes to live long and to live happily, let him act according to the following directions. For a comment upon this and the four ensuing verses, see the notes on <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.10-1Pet.3.12">1Pet 3:10-12</reference> (note).
entries.afe98c528eadbcaac8abb5034c6ed13f97d5d292: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen19668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19669" type="x-p"/> The righteous cry - There is no word in the present Hebrew text for righteous; but all the versions preserve it. I suppose it was lost through its similitude to the word צעקו tsaaku, they cry צעקו צדיקים tsaaku tsaddikim, the righteous cry.
entries.2e297081510d755b6b1d52a7ba43022e4cde0b00: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen19669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19670" type="x-p"/> A broken heart - נשברי לב nishberey Web, the heart broken to shivers. <div eID="gen19670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19671" type="x-p"/> A contrite spirit - דכאי רוח dakkeey ruach, "the beaten-out spirit." In both words the hammer is necessarily implied; in breaking to pieces the ore first, and then plating out the metal when it has been separated from the ore. This will call to the reader's remembrance <reference osisRef="Jer.23.29">Jer 23:29</reference> : "Is not my word like as a fire, saith the Lord? And like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?" The breaking to shivers, and beating out, are metaphorical expressions: so are the hammer and the rock. What the large hammer struck on a rock by a powerful hand would do, so does the word of the Lord when struck on the sinner's heart by the power of the Holy Spirit. The broken heart, and the contrite spirit, are two essential characteristics of true repentance.
entries.64e1a812ab22a1752ebbdbb22eae7b3bea18a70b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen19671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19672" type="x-p"/> Many are the afflictions of the righteous - No commander would do justice to a brave and skillful soldier, by refusing him opporbunities to put his skill and bravery to proof by combating with the adversary; or by preventing him from taking the post of danger when necessity required it. The righteous are God's soldiers. He suffers them to be tried, and sometimes to enter into the hottest of the battle and in their victory the power and influence of the grace of God is shown, as well as their faithfulness. <div eID="gen19672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19673" type="x-p"/> Delivereth him out of them all - He may well combat heartily, who knows that if he fight in the Lord, he shall necessarily be the conqueror.
entries.5bd290b502981010c720d17208add10af362acc0: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen19673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19674" type="x-p"/> He keepeth all his bones - He takes care of his life; and if he have scars, they are honorable ones.
entries.3521aff7f3fd482225ca334116656db8f8ebb7dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen19674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19675" type="x-p"/> Evil shall slay the wicked - The very thing in which they delight shall become their bane and their ruin. <div eID="gen19675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19676" type="x-p"/> They that hate the righteous - All persecutors of God's people shall be followed by the chilling blast of God's displeasure in this world; and if they repent not, shall perish everlastingly.
entries.25946c3bc628486b3d54038349825b36b6e2e94b: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen19676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19677" type="x-p"/> The Lord redeemeth - Both the life and soul of God's followers are ever in danger but God is continually redeeming both. <div eID="gen19677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19678" type="x-p"/> Shall be desolate - Literally, shall be guilty. They shall be preserved from sin, and neither forfeit life nor soul. This verse probably should come in after the fifth.
